records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source states pet toxicity for Tulbaghia violacea, so toxic_to_pets is left null (nothing borrowed from Allium). The NC State page for this exact name carries no Poison block and no Problem for Cats/Dogs tags, and gives no severity rating, symptom list or handling warning. Edibility as stated: NC State's Edibility field says "Flowers and leaves are edible (mild garlic flavor), and may be used in soups and salads."; its Description adds "The edible flowers have an oniony to peppery flavor and may be eaten raw or cooked."; MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics repeats the soups-and-salads sentence. Neither source gives times, doses or preparation conditions beyond that. MoBot notes "All parts of this plant emit a strong garlic odor" (a deer and rabbit resistance note, not a toxicity statement).
records.cool_rest_note: MoBot: in colder areas (St. Louis, Zone 6) container plants are brought indoors before first fall frost for overwintering in a bright, cool area (40-50 degrees F) with very minimal watering. This is overwintering advice for containers, not a damage-onset figure.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: none of the admissible pages read (NC State, MoBot, RHS) states toxicity to cats or dogs for Tulbaghia violacea; Allium toxicity deliberately not borrowed.

is_edible is true for flowers and leaves per NC State and MoBot; neither page gives preparation times or conditions beyond 'used in soups and salads' and 'eaten raw or cooked' (flowers). RHS does not address edibility.

outdoor_sun_exposure lists only full_sun: NC State's structured Light field also lists Partial Shade (2-6 hours direct sun), but MoBot's Sun field and RHS Position both say Full sun, and MoBot says plants 'will grow in part shade, but with decreased flowering' (a conditional tolerance). part_shade left out and disclosed here.

soil_drainage moderate rests on MoBot 'medium moisture, well-drained'; RHS's Moisture field reads Well-drained and NC State's Soil Drainage is the bare 'Good Drainage' with no Moist tag. RHS's 'Grows well in any moderately fertile, well-drained, loamy soil' sits after the genus blurb and reads as genus-level How to Grow text, so it is not cited. No source calls for sharp or sandy drainage with wet-soil intolerance, so fast was not used.

water_regime left null: MoBot says plants 'generally appreciate consistent moisture during the growing season' and NC State says 'do best with adequate moisture during the growing season' but also good drought tolerance; MoBot's structured Water: Medium is mid-scale. No watering statement maps cleanly to a regime token. MoBot gives 'very minimal watering' only for overwintering containers indoors.
soil_ph left null: RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling or floor can be set; NC State and MoBot give no pH.
soil_base garden_bed reflects in-ground use (MoBot: may be planted in the ground as a perennial); sources also describe container culture, so potting mix guidance is not given.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Container, Patio and Walkways (no Houseplants entry) over USDA zones 7a-10b; MoBot describes an outdoor tender perennial whose containers can be overwintered indoors, which is overwintering, not houseplant culture.
Hardiness is not a schema field: NC State lists USDA zones 7a-10b, MoBot Zone 7 to 10; RHS rates H3 (UK ratings). No chill-damage onset temperature is stated, so chill_damage_f is null.
attracts_pollinators null: no Attracts field on NC State, no pollinator tag on RHS, nothing in MoBot.
humidity, light footcandles, direct-sun hours, day/night temperatures, fertilizer, watering intervals not stated by admissible sources; left null.

Mature size from NC State Dimensions (Height 1-2 ft, Width 1-2 ft = 12-24 in each). MoBot gives Height 1.00 to 2.00 feet and Spread 0.75 to 1.00 feet (9-12 in spread), and RHS Max Height and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres; spread differs slightly between sources.

No Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was located; MoBot page was read via its plantfinder.mobot.org redirect, and ask.ifas.ufl.edu / plantfinder.mobot.org are hosts the live quote checker may skip.

records.name_note: Admissible sources with a dedicated page for this taxon split on the lead common name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized: Hardy Cyclamen, Ivy-leaved cyclamen, Persian violet; its description opens 'Hardy cyclamen is a tuberous herbaceous perennial in the primrose family (Primulaceae)'. RHS's plant profile shows ivy-leaved cyclamen as the common name under its Cyclamen hederifolium heading and lists Neapolitan cyclamen and sowbread as other common names. Hardy Cyclamen was chosen as the common_name because NC State's first-listed name is Hardy Cyclamen and its description text uses it; ivy-leaved cyclamen is the RHS lead name. RHS also lists Cyclamen neapolitanum under Synonyms. Distinct from Cyclamen persicum, the tender florist houseplant already in this catalog as Persian Cyclamen.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Plant Toolbox page for this exact name: its description says "This plant is toxic to humans, cats, dogs, and horses if ingested. Keep this plant out of the reach of children and pets." Its Problems list reads Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. The page-top summary says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." and links to the Poison block, which is headed 'Poisonous to Humans' and is human-scoped: Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "Salivation, vomiting, diarrhea. Following large ingestions of tubers: heart rhythm abnormalities, seizures, death"; Poison Toxic Principle: Terpenoid saponins; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Plant Type on the same page: Bulb, Herbaceous Perennial. The page gives no per-animal symptom list or severity; the symptom list sits in the human-scoped block. RHS page for this exact name, Potentially harmful field: "Ornamental bulbs, not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling"; its Pets line says "Ornamental bulbs; not to be eaten" and names no animal, so it was not used for toxic_to_pets. The two admissible sources do not disagree on scope.
unknowns: is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Container, Naturalized Area, Patio, Small Space and Woodland (no Houseplants entry) over USDA zones 5a-9b, and treats it as a hardy outdoor woodland perennial. Do not carry over Cyclamen persicum florist/indoor care.
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page for Cyclamen hederifolium (kempercode s710) could not be fetched in this session (connection/certificate failure), so no MoBot content was used or cited.

water_regime left null: NC State's only watering statement ('It is best to keep them on the dry side when dormant') covers dormancy only; its 'humus-rich, moist soil' is a soil adjective, not a watering instruction. RHS says only 'Avoid excessive summer moisture'. No growing-season watering instruction found, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and both day-interval fields are also null.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), all open-ended bands, and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no closed bound is supported.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's '2-6 hours' appears only in the site-wide Partial Shade light-category legend text on the Light field, not in species-specific prose; no species prose gives an hour figure. RHS lists Position Partial shade only (and aspects of all four compass directions, exposure Sheltered).

No source gave an onset chill-damage temperature, day/night temperature range, humidity figure, light foot-candle figure or fertilizing schedule; those fields are null. NC State USDA zones 5a-9b and RHS rating H5 are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
is_edible set false from NC State ('toxic to humans, cats, dogs, and horses if ingested') and RHS ('Ornamental bulbs, not to be eaten'); no source describes any food use.

Pet toxicity: NC State names cats, dogs and horses explicitly in its description sentence and Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags; the symptom list is in a human-scoped block and the page gives no per-animal symptoms or severity for pets. RHS's Pets line names no animal.

mature size comes from NC State's structured Dimensions block (Height 0 ft. 4 in. - 0 ft. 6 in. = 4-6 in; Width 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 0 in. = 6-12 in). RHS gives Max Height Up to 10 cm (about 3.9 in; open at the low end) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), which differ from NC State; NC State used.
RHS Position says Partial shade, matching NC State's Partial Shade; both mapped to part_shade only.

records.name_note: RHS leads with Jersey lily (shown under the H1) and lists belladonna lily under Other common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Amaryllis Lily, August Lily, Belladonna Lily, Jersey Lily, March Lily, Naked Lady, Resurrection Lily), and its description prose calls the plant 'Naked lady'. Jersey Lily is the lead name on RHS and also appears on NC State's list, so it is used here. The bare name Amaryllis is avoided. NC State's often-confused-with module names Hippeastrum and Lycoris squamigera.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State: the page-top summary says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." and links 'See below' to the Poison block, which is headed "Poisonous to Humans:" and gives Poison Severity: Low, so the severity rating is human-scoped. Poison Symptoms: "Vomiting (not horses), depression, diarrhea, abdominal pain, hypersalivation, anorexia, tremors. The plant toxicity is more pronounced in pets, especially cats." Poison Toxic Principle: "Lycorine and other alkaliods" (the source's own spelling). Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Separately from that human-scoped block, NC State's Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, and its Tags carry #problem for cats, #problem for dogs and #problem for horses. Wildlife Value: "Toxic to animals". Plant Type: Bulb. RHS: under Potentially harmful, "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". RHS's Pets line names no animal and is not used as cat or dog evidence. Scope: NC State's symptom list excludes horses for vomiting, while its tags still list horses as a problem; no admissible source gives a dose.
unknowns: No Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page for Amaryllis belladonna was found (MoBot only mentions it on other taxa's pages), and UF/IFAS, Clemson, PSU, UMD and UGA pages found were multi-species or genus-level, so only NC State and RHS dedicated pages are used.

is_houseplant true rests on NC State's Landscape Location list, which includes Houseplants alongside Container, Patio and Woodland. Its prose and RHS's page otherwise describe an outdoor bulb (beds, borders, containers, lifted below zone 8), so the single structured tag is the only indoor statement; the landing gate does not admit null.
soil_drainage left null: NC State gives a bare Good Drainage and RHS gives Moist but well-drained or Well-drained, which is ambiguous between moderate and fast.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State gives the closed Neutral (6.0-8.0) band while RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral as acceptable.

water_regime and the day-interval fields left null: neither page gives a watering instruction. NC State's drought tolerance is a trait, not a watering statement. NC State's Bulb Storage temperature (55-70 F) is a storage figure, not a growing or damage temperature.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State's USDA zones 3a-10b and its advice to lift bulbs below zone 8, and RHS's H4 rating, are not damage-onset temperatures.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 6-or-more-hours figure is the generic light-category legend, not species prose.

Mature size conflict: NC State's Dimensions block gives 2-3 ft for height and width (used, as 24-36 in); RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread of 0.1-0.5 metres (about 3.9-19.7 in), which disagrees with NC State and is not used.
is_edible is false from RHS's 'Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten' statement; NC State does not address eating.
NC State lists the cat, dog and horse tags separately from its human-scoped Poison block, and no admissible source gives a dose or a cat-versus-dog severity beyond 'especially cats'.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page is headed Tecomaria capensis, lists Cape Honeysuckle as its only common name, and lists Tecoma capensis among its 'Previously known as' names. RHS's dedicated page is headed Tecoma capensis, with Cape honeysuckle as its rendered common name, lists Tecomaria capensis as a synonym, and gives Name Status as Correct, so Tecoma capensis is recorded as the accepted name. NC State places it in the trumpetvine family (Bignoniaceae).
unknowns: Toxicity: neither the NC State page nor the RHS page for this taxon carries a poison or pet-toxicity block, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. No non-toxicity is asserted.
Edibility: NC State mentions only medicinal bark and leaf use in southern Africa, not food use, so is_edible is null.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Landscape Location lists Coastal, Container and Vertical Spaces (no Houseplants entry) over USDA zones 9a-11b. RHS suggests growing in a container and overwintering indoors, and NC State notes spider mites or whiteflies may occur if kept indoors, but neither calls it a houseplant.
Invasiveness: NC State says it was naturalized in Australia and is now considered invasive, and its Problems field lists Weedy. This is regional and not a global claim.

Size sources disagree: NC State gives height 3-10 ft (36-120 in) and width 7-10 ft (84-120 in), used as the anchor. RHS gives Max Height 2.5-4 metres (about 98-157 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (about 59-98 in), reached in 5-10 years.

Sun: NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours), and its prose says 'The Cape Honeysuckle blooms in full sun to partial shade.' RHS's Position field lists Full sun only, so part_shade is not set; full_sun is supported by both.
Soil pH left null: NC State lists acid, alkaline and neutral, and RHS lists acid or alkaline or neutral, all open-ended, so no ceiling or floor can be set.

water_regime is null: NC State says only that the soil should be moist and well-drained, which is a soil description, not a watering instruction. Drought tolerance is a trait and not a watering rule. No fertilizer, humidity, indoor temperature or light-meter data was found in admissible sources.
chill_damage_f 25 is NC State's figure at which leaves and branches die back. NC State's USDA zones 9-11 and RHS's UK rating H1C are not damage-onset figures and were not used.
NC State's Woody Plant Leaf Characteristics lists both Broadleaf Evergreen and Deciduous, and its description says it is evergreen in most regions but loses leaves in colder climates.

MoBot (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be reached from this session (TLS/proxy failure), and no dedicated UF/IFAS EDIS, Clemson, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for this taxon was found, so only NC State and RHS are cited.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's species page leads with glory lily and lists flame lily only under Other common names. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, beginning with Cat's Claw, and includes both Flame Lily and Glory Lily. Glory Lily is chosen because it is RHS's lead name; Flame Lily is also a valid common name on both pages. NC State lists Gloriosa rothschildiana as a previous name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page-top summary says "This plant has high severity poison characteristics." Its Poison block, headed 'Poisonous to Humans' (human-scoped): Poison Severity: High; Poison Symptoms: "Numbness of lips, tongue, and throat, thirst, fever, bloody vomiting, bloody diarrhea, difficult breathing, convulsions, shock, multi-organ damage, bone marrow suppression, respiratory depression, and cardiovascular collapse."; Poison Toxic Principle: "Alkaloids (colchicine and others) and resins"; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. NC State prose: "All parts of this plant are poisonous, especially tubers (thickened roots), which resemble yams. This plant is highly toxic and may be fatal if eaten." and "If ingested, all parts of the plant are toxic to cats, dogs, horses, livestock, and humans." NC State Problems field (separate from the Poison block): Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses; Plant Type: Bulb, Poisonous, Vine; Tags include #poisonous, #problem for cats, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses, #poisonous if ingested, #problem for cattle, #problem for children. NC State Edibility: "Toxic when ingested." Ethnobotany: "The plant contains colchicine and is used in medicine to treat arthritis, gout, and inflammation. Colchicine is extracted from the seeds." RHS Potentially harmful: "TOXIC if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" and "TOXIC to pets (dogs)". Scope: RHS names dogs only for pets; NC State names cats, dogs and horses (and livestock and humans). No admissible page says the tubers have been fatally mistaken for yams; NC State says only that they resemble yams.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State: prefers moderate daytime temperatures and cool nights; tubers are dormant over the winter and, if lifted, are stored in peat or vermiculite at 40 to 50°F. RHS: keep tubers dry in winter.
unknowns: Synonym Gloriosa modesta: no admissible species-page source found stating it; RHS lists the synonym Gloriosa plantii and NC State lists Gloriosa rothschildiana only.

No Missouri Botanical Garden page for the species itself was found; the MoBot Plant Finder entry located is cultivar-only (Rothschildiana) and was not used. No Clemson, PSU, UMD or UGA species page found.
UF/IFAS EP648 has a Gloriosa section but is a multi-species publication, so it was not used; it was not cited.
toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State (cats, dogs, horses, livestock, humans) and RHS (dogs only).
The claim that tubers were fatally mistaken for yams is not on any admissible page; NC State only says the tubers resemble yams and the plant may be fatal if eaten.
chill_damage_f null: no source states a damage-onset temperature; NC State hardiness zones 8 to 12 are a survival rating, not onset.
day_f_min 70 and night_f_min 60 are lower bounds read from NC State's 'in the 70s' and '60s at night'; no maximum is stated.
soil_ph_min/max null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), which is open-ended at the bottom, and Neutral (6.0-8.0); RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral, so no closed range is supported.

water_regime keep_moist rests on RHS 'Water freely once in growth' and NC State's moist soil; NC State warns overwatering can cause root rot and that tubers rot in moist conditions over winter, and RHS says keep tubers dry in winter, so dormant-season watering is the opposite. RHS Moisture 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' is a soil field.
fertilize_interval_days null: RHS says 'apply a balanced liquid fertiliser every two weeks', a word-based cadence not converted to a number; strength and months not stated.

direct_sun_hours_max null: only NC State's generic light-legend hours exist. RHS Position is full sun only (Aspect: South–facing or East–facing or West–facing); NC State's Light field adds Partial Shade and its prose says 'Needs protection from the hot sun and will benefit from afternoon shade.'

Size: NC State Dimensions give height 5-6 ft and width 1-3 ft for this climber; RHS gives Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in); NC State used as anchor. Height is on a trellis for a climbing plant.
Humidity and light foot-candles: no admissible source states them.

records.name_note: RHS's page for Canna indica shows Indian shot as the common name under its heading. NC State's Common Name(s) list for the same taxon is alphabetized, begins with Achira and also contains Indian Shot, so Indian Shot, the name both dedicated pages carry and RHS leads with, is used as the common name. This record is Canna indica only, not the hybrid Canna × generalis, already in this catalog as Canna Lily.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Canna indica page has no Poison block, no poison-part list and no symptom list. Its structured tags (same block, listed in full) read: "#showy flowers #red flowers #tropical feel #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #showy leaves #large leaves #pollinator plant #rhizomatous #edible roots #cottage garden #container plant #perennial #patio". Plant Type on that page is Bulb and Perennial. The cat and dog non-toxic tags are NC State's own tags on the Canna indica page; ASPCA's non-toxic listing is filed under the hybrid Canna x generalis and is not used. Edibility (NC State, Edibility field): "It has been cultivated as a food crop for over 4000 years in Central and South America. The tubers may be eaten raw or cooked." NC State also says a starch suitable for baking is produced by pounding or grinding the roots, called achira, and the leaves are used to wrap tamales and fed to livestock. NC State gives no cooking time or other preparation condition for the tubers.
unknowns: Invasiveness: no dedicated admissible Canna indica page states it. The only statement found is on the UF/IFAS Canna flaccida (golden canna) publication FP102, which says Indian shot is considered invasive in Australia, South Africa and many Pacific Islands, and that there is no evidence it has become a problem in Florida. That is a different species' page, so it is recorded here and not used for any field.
No Missouri Botanical Garden species page for Canna indica was found (only Canna group, aquatic group and cultivar pages), so MoBot is not used.

is_houseplant false: NC State's Plant Type is Bulb and Perennial over USDA zones 8a-11b and its Landscape Location lists Container and Patio only; RHS lists Conservatory and Greenhouse among suggested planting locations, but neither states indoor houseplant use.

Edibility: NC State says the tubers may be eaten raw or cooked and gives no cooking time or preparation conditions. No admissible source states a cooked-only condition. Nothing admissible addresses toxicity of any part to people beyond NC State's pet and horse non-toxic tags.
toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs tags. No admissible source for this exact taxon gives a symptom list or poison-part list.

water_regime and the watering-interval fields are null. records.name_note: Solanum jasminoides is a former name that resolves here: NC State says "The species name was previously Solanum jasminoides" and lists Solanum dietrichiae and Solanum jasminoides under Previously known as, and RHS lists Solanum jasminoides (and the cultivar name Solanum jasminoides 'Bleu') under Synonyms. Sources differ slightly on the lead common name. NC State's Common Name(s) list reads Climbing Nightshade, Jasmine Nightshade, Potato Climber, Potato Vine in alphabetical order, while its Description prose opens with "Potato vine". RHS's plant profile shows potato vine as the common name under its Solanum laxum heading and lists Japanese nightshade and jasmine nightshade under Other common names. Potato Vine is used as the primary name because RHS and the NC State Description both lead with it. Distinct from Solanum tuberosum (Potato), Trachelospermum jasminoides (Star Jasmine) and Ipomoea batatas (sweet potato vine).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu, Solanum laxum page) only; the RHS page for this species carries no toxicity statement. NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity High (the page also says "This plant has high severity poison characteristics."), Poison Toxic Principle "Solanine alkaloid", and Poison Part: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Its Poison Symptoms text, verbatim: "If ingested, the leaves or berries are dangerous to children and pets. The vines are very toxic and may damage the kidneys, brain, heart, and liver. Symptoms of alkaloid poisoning include confusion, dilated pupils, diarrhea, vomiting, and weakness. The plant irritates the skin when handled. It is best to wear protective clothing and gloves." The block also lists Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Separately from that human-scoped block, the page's Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. Plant Type field: Poisonous, Shrub, Vine. Edibility field: "Non-edible. The plant is toxic if ingested." Full tag list as rendered: #problem for cats #problem for horses #problem for dogs #vine #skin irritation #black fruits #white flowers #blue fruits #shrub #non-edible berries #problem for children #perennial vines #fragrant flowers #neutral pH #garden walls #hummingbird friendly #alkaline soils tolerant #cottage garden #deer resistant #easy to grow #poisonous #fast growing #frost tender #fence #poisonous if ingested #trellis #climber #twining. The Insects, Diseases, and Other Plant Problems text adds that the plant "is risky for pets and children". The Poison Symptoms sentence names the leaves or berries as dangerous, while the Poison Part list is unrestricted (all seven parts); the two scopes are both on the same NC State page and are not reconciled there.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden: no Solanum laxum page could be loaded (the Plant Finder host failed to connect in this run, and searches surfaced no page for this exact name), so MoBot contributed nothing. Clemson HGIC returned HTTP 403, the UF/IFAS EDIS page tried returned HTTP 410, and no dedicated page on the other admissible domains was found.

toxic_to_pets is true on NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags and its Poison Symptoms sentence ('dangerous to children and pets'). The High severity rating comes from NC State's human-scoped Poisonous to Humans block. No admissible source gives a pet-specific symptom list or dose. RHS has no toxicity statement.

Poison scope within NC State: the Poison Symptoms sentence names 'the leaves or berries', while the Poison Part list covers flowers, fruits, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds and stems. No admissible source restricts the toxicity to the fruit only.
is_edible is false per NC State's Edibility field (non-edible, toxic if ingested). No other admissible source addresses eating.

is_houseplant is true only on NC State's Landscape Location listing 'Houseplants' and its statement that the plant can be over-wintered in a sunny window. The plant is chiefly an outdoor climber (hardy to zones 9a-11b per NC State, H4 per RHS), and NC State describes it as 'vulnerable to freezing temperatures'.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State says the plant 'is tolerant of temperatures down to 20 degrees F' in mild winter climates, and gives zone 9a-11b. RHS gives hardiness rating H4. Both are hardiness or survival figures, not an onset-of-damage temperature.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field lists both 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and its prose says 'full sun to light shade'. RHS's structured Position lists Full sun only (Aspect South–facing or West–facing), so part_shade was not set. direct_sun_hours_max is left null because the only hour figures on the NC State page come from the site-wide light legend.
soil_ph_min 6.0 is the floor of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band. soil_ph_max is left null because NC State lists Alkaline (>8.0), which is open-ended, and RHS lists pH as Alkaline or Neutral.

soil_base garden_bed is inferred from the in-ground culture NC State describes ('fertile well-drained soil'). NC State also notes it can be grown in pots or window boxes, and RHS gives a separate under-glass compost note that was not used because it may be genus-level text.

water_regime and all watering interval fields are left null. NC State says 'moderate moisture' and lists Good Drainage plus Moist; RHS says 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. These are soil-moisture descriptors for an in-ground climber, not watering instructions.
Humidity, indoor light, temperature ranges, fertilizer and cool-rest data: no admissible source page found with this information, left null.

Mature size is NC State's Dimensions block (Height 20 ft. - 30 ft., Width 5 ft. - 6 ft., converted to inches: 240-360 and 60-72). RHS lists Max Height 4-8 metres (157-315 in) and Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98-157 in), so the two sources differ. NC State also says stems can grow up to 50 feet long. For a twining climber these heights depend on the support.
attracts_pollinators is true from NC State's Attracts field (Hummingbirds) and Wildlife Value sentence. RHS shows no pollinator tag on the page text retrieved.
